messages.content: I want speech–gesture reference resolution to use a gesture when it actually determines what someone is referring to, without mistaking speaker-specific correlations for gesture-dependent meaning. The timing between speech and gesture may be uncertain.

The goal is to resolve references using information from both speech and gesture while distinguishing a meaningful gesture cue from a pattern associated with a particular speaker. It should not depend on speech and gesture lining up at one exact moment. Those are aims for the system, not claims about what it can already do.
What would show that gesture is adding something beyond speech alone?

On gesture-dependent references from unseen speakers, the target is an accuracy gain of at least 10 percentage points over speech-only models. The comparison matters: it calls for improvement specifically where the gesture is needed to resolve the reference, and for that improvement to carry over to speakers the system has not seen.
Is “10 percentage points” the same as a 10 percent relative improvement?

No. Percentage points describe an absolute difference between accuracy rates. The requirement is at least a 10-percentage-point accuracy gain over speech-only models, not merely a 10 percent relative increase.
Why specify unseen speakers rather than just gesture-dependent references?

The unseen-speaker condition keeps the comparison focused on whether gesture helps beyond correlations tied to particular speakers. An accuracy gain confined to familiar speakers would not satisfy the stated target for gesture-dependent references from unseen speakers.
Does that mean speaker information can never be relevant?

The goal does not impose a blanket ban on speaker information. It asks the resolver to distinguish gesture-dependent meaning from speaker-specific correlations, so that apparent success on a reference is not simply tied to who is speaking rather than to the gesture’s contribution.
What happens if a gesture is present but irrelevant to the reference?

That is part of the robustness requirement. Under irrelevant-gesture substitutions, accuracy degradation must be limited to 5 percentage points. The aim is not to treat every visible gesture as decisive; an irrelevant substituted gesture should not cause a larger drop than that limit.
And how does uncertain timing enter the requirement?

Accuracy degradation must also be limited to 5 percentage points under ±300-millisecond audiovisual offsets. The plus-or-minus notation covers offsets in either temporal direction: the speech and visual signals need not have perfect timing for the resolver to remain within the stated degradation limit.
So the gain and the robustness limit are two different targets?

Yes. The gain target is at least 10 percentage points over speech-only models on gesture-dependent references from unseen speakers. Separately, the robustness target limits accuracy degradation to 5 percentage points under irrelevant-gesture substitutions and ±300-millisecond audiovisual offsets. A strong gain in the first condition would not, by itself, establish the required robustness.
Could I describe this as learning to ignore gestures?

Not across the board. Ignoring gesture altogether would work against the required gain on gesture-dependent references. The distinction is whether the gesture contributes to resolving the reference: it should help when it carries needed meaning, without an irrelevant substitution unduly disrupting the result.
Does the ±300-millisecond condition say exactly how speech and gesture should be matched?

No. It states a timing-robustness condition, not a matching procedure. The objective is to resolve speech–gesture references under uncertain cross-modal timing while keeping accuracy degradation within 5 percentage points under the specified audiovisual offsets.
What about testing an irrelevant substitution and an audiovisual offset at the same time?

The stated requirement names irrelevant-gesture substitutions and ±300-millisecond audiovisual offsets, but it does not specify an additional result for their simultaneous combination. It is best to keep the stated limits intact without adding a combined-condition requirement.
If the system meets the gain over speech-only models, can I say it has distinguished gesture meaning from speaker-specific correlations?

You can say that the gain on gesture-dependent references from unseen speakers is one of the required outcomes for that goal. The goal also explicitly calls for distinguishing gesture-dependent meaning from speaker-specific correlations and for limiting degradation under the two robustness conditions. The gain alone should not be presented as the whole objective.
Please put the complete target in one sentence.

Enable speech–gesture reference resolution that distinguishes gesture-dependent meaning from speaker-specific correlations under uncertain cross-modal timing, achieves at least a 10-percentage-point accuracy gain over speech-only models on gesture-dependent references from unseen speakers, and limits accuracy degradation to 5 percentage points under irrelevant-gesture substitutions and ±300-millisecond audiovisual offsets.
How would you propose training ShiftGuard for the speech–gesture reference-resolution goal?

The proposal is to train ShiftGuard with four complementary elements: speaker-adversarial embeddings, ±300 ms temporal marginalization, irrelevant-gesture invariance, and label-updated relevant-gesture swaps. Together, they address the distinction between gesture-dependent meaning and speaker-specific correlations, as well as uncertainty about when the speech and gesture align. This is a training proposal, not a report of results.
What is the speaker-adversarial part meant to do?

Speaker-adversarial embeddings are meant to make the learned representation less reliant on cues that identify a speaker. That supports the goal of resolving a reference from the speech and any meaningful gesture, rather than from a correlation particular to the person speaking. The proposal does not specify an architecture or claim that every trace of speaker information will be removed.
Would that mean the system should ignore differences in how people speak?

Not necessarily. The point is to resist speaker-specific shortcuts when interpreting the reference, not to assert that all variation between speakers is useless. The proposal names speaker-adversarial embeddings, but it does not spell out a rule for discarding every speaker-related feature.
What does ±300 ms temporal marginalization mean here?

It means training ShiftGuard to account for uncertainty in audiovisual alignment across a range extending 300 milliseconds in either temporal direction. Rather than making the reference depend on one presumed exact alignment, the proposal allows for possible speech–gesture timing offsets within that range. It does not specify a particular marginalization calculation or claim measured robustness yet.
Is it just shifting everything by 300 milliseconds?

No. The ± sign indicates timing uncertainty in both directions, not one fixed shift of 300 milliseconds. “Temporal marginalization” also points to accounting for possible alignments rather than treating a single displaced alignment as the only one. The precise training procedure is not specified in the proposal.
Then what does irrelevant-gesture invariance require the model to learn?

It is intended to keep a reference-resolution decision from changing just because an irrelevant gesture is substituted. If the gesture does not determine the reference, replacing it should not be mistaken for a change in what the speech refers to. That is the intended training behavior; the proposal does not say it has already been achieved.
But if you make the model invariant to gesture substitutions, won't it stop using gestures altogether?

That is why the proposal distinguishes irrelevant gestures from relevant ones. Irrelevant-gesture invariance is not a blanket instruction to ignore all gestures. The label-updated relevant-gesture swaps provide the complementary case: when a swapped gesture is relevant to the reference, the associated label is updated to reflect that gesture's meaning.
Can you clarify why the labels need updating for relevant-gesture swaps?

Keeping the original label after a meaningfully relevant gesture swap could tell the model to overlook the very cue it needs to use. Updating the label makes the training example consistent with the reference indicated by the swapped relevant gesture. The proposal identifies that relationship; it does not prescribe which gestures to swap or how examples are selected.
So are the two swap ideas opposites?

They teach different responses to different kinds of gesture change. With an irrelevant-gesture substitution, the desired reference interpretation remains stable. With a relevant-gesture swap, the label is updated to match the reference indicated by the relevant gesture. The contrast is about whether the gesture carries meaning for the reference, not about treating all visual changes alike.
Does a label-updated relevant-gesture swap imply that every swap must produce a different label?

The stated proposal requires the label to be updated appropriately for the swapped relevant gesture. It does not separately specify that every individual swap must produce a different label. The essential point is not to retain a label that conflicts with the reference indicated by the relevant gesture.
How do those gesture-related elements connect to the speaker-adversarial embeddings?

They address complementary risks. The gesture-related elements distinguish changes that should matter for a reference from changes that should not. The speaker-adversarial embeddings aim to discourage using speaker-specific correlations as a substitute for that distinction. Their proposed combination is meant to favor the gesture's actual contribution when the gesture is relevant.
And temporal marginalization is separate from whether the gesture is relevant?

Yes. Relevance concerns whether a gesture contributes to identifying the referent; temporal marginalization concerns uncertainty about how the speech and gesture line up in time. A gesture could be relevant even when its exact timing relative to speech is uncertain, so the proposal includes both elements.
Are you saying ShiftGuard already meets the accuracy targets we discussed?

No. This node proposes how to train ShiftGuard; it provides no experimental outcome. The earlier goal sets performance targets, while these four elements are proposed training ingredients aimed at that goal. Their inclusion alone does not establish any accuracy gain or robustness limit.
Can we at least say which ingredient is responsible for a particular percentage-point gain?

Not from the proposal alone. It states the four training elements but gives no measured contribution for any one of them. Assigning a percentage-point effect to speaker-adversarial embeddings, temporal marginalization, irrelevant-gesture invariance, or relevant-gesture swaps would add an unsupported result.
Give me a concise formulation that keeps the proposal, rather than its hoped-for results, front and center.

Train ShiftGuard using speaker-adversarial embeddings, temporal marginalization over ±300 ms audiovisual timing uncertainty, invariance to irrelevant-gesture substitutions, and relevant-gesture swaps whose labels are updated to reflect the swapped gesture's reference.
Can label-updated gesture swaps preserve referent-bearing motion while speaker-adversarial training removes identity cues under ±300 ms jitter?

That is the open question. The two training elements are intended to act on different information: label-updated gesture swaps should keep the motion that matters for identifying the referent useful, while speaker-adversarial training should discourage reliance on cues to the speaker’s identity. The ±300 ms jitter adds uncertainty about how the gesture and speech line up. The proposal does not establish that ShiftGuard can maintain all three properties at once.
What do you mean by preserving referent-bearing motion if the gesture is being swapped?

Preserving it means preserving the model’s ability to use motion that bears on the reference, not keeping the original gesture unchanged. When a relevant gesture is swapped, the label is updated to reflect the reference indicated by that gesture. The intended lesson is that a meaningful change in gesture can change the reference, rather than that gesture changes should always be ignored.
Does updating the label alone ensure the model attends to the motion?

No. An updated label makes the training example’s stated reference consistent with the relevant gesture swap, but it does not by itself prove which cues the model uses. The question asks whether the referent-bearing motion remains available and influential alongside the pressure to remove identity cues and tolerate timing uncertainty.
Why might speaker-adversarial training make that difficult?

Conceptually, a training signal that discourages speaker identity cues must distinguish those cues from motion that conveys the referent. If the representation treats them as inseparable, suppressing identity information could also suppress useful motion information. That is a possible tension raised by the question, not an observed failure.
So speaker-adversarial training is not meant to erase the gesture?

Right. Its intended role is to reduce reliance on speaker-identity cues, not to remove the gesture’s reference-bearing content. The question is whether that distinction can be maintained in the learned representation; the proposed training ingredients alone do not guarantee it.
Where does the ±300 ms jitter complicate the distinction?

It makes the speech–gesture alignment uncertain by as much as 300 milliseconds in either direction. A useful gesture cue still has to contribute to resolving the reference when its timing relative to speech is displaced. The question is whether that timing tolerance can coexist with retaining the meaningful motion and reducing identity cues.
Is the concern that jitter changes what the gesture means?

Not necessarily. The stated concern is uncertain cross-modal timing: the gesture may be offset relative to speech even if its referent-bearing content is still important. Nothing in the question says that a ±300 ms offset itself changes the correct referent.
Could a system simply rely less on all visual information to cope with the jitter?

It might become less sensitive to visual information in general, but that would not answer the question favorably if it also stopped using referent-bearing motion. The proposed balance is narrower: tolerate uncertain timing and discourage identity cues while remaining responsive to relevant gesture content.
How is that different from irrelevant-gesture invariance?

Irrelevant-gesture invariance concerns changes that should not affect the reference. Label-updated relevant-gesture swaps concern changes that do bear on the reference and therefore call for an updated label. The present question focuses on whether the latter can preserve useful motion information despite speaker-adversarial training and ±300 ms timing jitter.
When you say identity cues, do you mean a known speaker label has to be predicted first?

No such step is specified. “Identity cues” here means information associated with who is speaking that could support a speaker-specific correlation rather than resolution from the meaningful gesture. The question does not define an identity-prediction procedure or an implementation for the adversarial training.
Could the label-updated swaps themselves eliminate identity cues?

That is not stated. Their specified role is to keep the label aligned with a relevant swapped gesture, encouraging sensitivity to referent-bearing motion. Speaker-adversarial training is the proposed element directed at identity cues. Whether the elements work together as intended remains open.
Is there a contradiction between changing the label for a relevant gesture and tolerating temporal jitter?

There is no necessary contradiction in their stated purposes. The updated label concerns what reference the relevant gesture indicates; the jitter concerns uncertainty in when that gesture occurs relative to speech. The unresolved issue is whether ShiftGuard can use the meaning-bearing motion reliably when both training pressures are present.
Does ±300 ms mean the gesture always occurs exactly 300 milliseconds early or late?

No. The ±300 ms condition expresses an offset range in both directions, not a requirement that every offset be exactly at an endpoint. The question is about preserving the distinction under that timing uncertainty, not about one fixed displacement.
What would a positive answer to the question actually mean?

It would mean that the training approach maintains sensitivity to motion that changes the referent when the relevant gesture and its label are changed, while reducing reliance on speaker-identity cues, even with audiovisual timing jitter within ±300 ms. That describes the capability being asked about; it does not claim the capability has been demonstrated.
And what should we avoid assuming before there is an answer?

We should not assume that label updates alone preserve the useful motion, that speaker-adversarial training cleanly removes identity cues without affecting that motion, or that timing tolerance follows automatically from either one. The question asks whether those desired effects can coexist under ±300 ms jitter.
Can you restate the question without turning it into a claim?

Can ShiftGuard use label-updated relevant-gesture swaps to retain referent-bearing motion, while speaker-adversarial training reduces identity cues, when speech and gesture are subject to ±300 ms timing jitter?
What is the hypothesis for ShiftGuard?

The hypothesis is that ShiftGuard’s label-updated gesture swaps and speaker-adversarial training will yield at least a 10-percentage-point accuracy gain over speech-only models on unseen-speaker GestureRef, while limiting accuracy loss to at most 5 percentage points under ±300 ms jitter and irrelevant-gesture swaps. Those are predicted outcomes, not reported results.
How does that relate to the question about preserving motion while removing identity cues?

It gives that question a performance prediction. If the relevant gesture swaps help retain referent-bearing motion and the adversarial training reduces reliance on speaker identity cues, the hypothesis predicts a substantial advantage over speech alone for unseen speakers. The small-loss condition asks whether that advantage can coexist with tolerance to uncertain timing and irrelevant gesture changes. The hypothesis does not establish that the proposed mechanisms work as intended.
Does “at least a 10-point gain” mean ShiftGuard must reach 10 percent accuracy?

No. It means its accuracy would be at least 10 percentage points higher than that of speech-only models on unseen-speaker GestureRef. The hypothesis does not specify an absolute accuracy for either ShiftGuard or the speech-only comparison.
Why is the speech-only comparison important here?

It asks whether ShiftGuard’s use of gesture-related information improves reference resolution beyond what speech alone provides. The stated prediction is a gain over speech-only models, not simply a particular accuracy in isolation. Because the condition is unseen-speaker GestureRef, the gain is also meant to hold when the speakers are unseen.
Can I say the hypothesis predicts that speaker-adversarial training by itself produces the whole gain?

No. The hypothesis attributes the predicted outcome to ShiftGuard’s label-updated swaps and speaker-adversarial training together. It does not assign a separate percentage-point contribution to either element or say that one alone is sufficient.
What exactly are the label-updated swaps expected to contribute?

Their proposed role is to let a relevant gesture change the reference without leaving the original label attached to the changed meaning. In the hypothesis, they are part of the reason ShiftGuard might remain sensitive to referent-bearing motion. That is an explanation of the proposed mechanism, not evidence that the motion has in fact been preserved.
And what is speaker-adversarial training expected to contribute?

It is intended to reduce reliance on speaker-identity cues, so that the predicted gain on unseen-speaker GestureRef reflects reference-relevant information rather than a shortcut tied to particular speakers. The hypothesis does not assert that identity cues have already been removed or specify how completely they could be removed.
Does the hypothesis prove that the model distinguishes a meaningful gesture from a speaker-specific pattern?

No. That distinction is central to what the proposed training is meant to achieve, and the unseen-speaker accuracy comparison is one predicted outcome. But a hypothesis about that outcome is not a demonstration that ShiftGuard has learned the intended distinction.
What does the 5-point part cover?

It predicts no more than a 5-percentage-point accuracy loss under ±300 ms jitter and irrelevant-gesture swaps. That is a robustness prediction alongside the predicted gain over speech-only models. It should not be restated as a 5 percent relative loss or as a claim that there is no loss at all.
Is the jitter one fixed 300-millisecond delay?

No. “±300 ms” refers to timing variation extending 300 milliseconds in either direction. The hypothesis is about limited accuracy loss under that audiovisual timing uncertainty, not only under one fixed delay.
What does an irrelevant-gesture swap test in this hypothesis?

It tests whether changing a gesture that is irrelevant to the reference causes undue disruption. The predicted loss is at most 5 percentage points under such swaps. That is different from a label-updated relevant-gesture swap, where the gesture bears on the reference and the label is updated accordingly.
Could I treat relevant and irrelevant swaps as interchangeable because both involve replacing a gesture?

No. Their relevance to the reference is the distinction. A label-updated relevant-gesture swap is meant to preserve the connection between a meaningful gesture and its indicated referent. An irrelevant-gesture swap is a robustness condition: the change should not unduly affect reference resolution. Treating them as interchangeable would erase what the hypothesis is trying to separate.
Does the 5-point limit refer to the gain over speech-only models?

The statement gives two different quantities: a gain of at least 10 percentage points over speech-only models on unseen-speaker GestureRef, and an accuracy loss of at most 5 percentage points under the stated perturbations. It does not explicitly define the comparison used to calculate the loss, so I would not invent a more specific baseline for it.
Is the hypothesis saying that jitter and irrelevant swaps are always applied together?

It names both ±300 ms jitter and irrelevant-gesture swaps as conditions under which loss should remain within 5 percentage points. It does not specify whether they are evaluated simultaneously, separately, or both, so the wording should not add a combined-condition claim.
What if there is a 10-point gain but a larger loss under jitter?

That would match the predicted gain but not the hypothesis’s predicted robustness under ±300 ms jitter. Both numerical conditions matter; satisfying one does not imply satisfying the other. This is a conditional reading of the hypothesis, not a statement about any observed ShiftGuard result.
What if the loss is within five points for irrelevant swaps but not for the timing variation?
Then the irrelevant-swap part of the prediction would hold while the ±300 ms jitter part would not. The hypothesis includes both, and neither should be silently dropped when describing it.
Can we infer from this that ShiftGuard has already been tested on GestureRef?

No. Naming unseen-speaker GestureRef specifies where the accuracy gain is predicted. The node supplies a hypothesis, not a completed evaluation, measured accuracy, or finding that the thresholds have been met.
Would it be accurate to call the 10-point threshold a proposed mechanism?

No. The at-least-10-percentage-point gain is a predicted performance outcome relative to speech-only models. Label-updated gesture swaps and speaker-adversarial training are the named training elements in the hypothesis; the accuracy threshold describes what they are hypothesized to yield together.
Does this hypothesis specify a new model architecture or a way to calculate the loss?

It does not. It names ShiftGuard and the two training elements associated with the prediction, plus the accuracy thresholds and conditions. It leaves architectural details and the precise loss calculation unstated.
Give me a careful one-sentence version that makes its status clear.

The hypothesis is that ShiftGuard’s label-updated gesture swaps and speaker-adversarial training will produce at least a 10-percentage-point accuracy gain over speech-only models on unseen-speaker GestureRef, with no more than a 5-percentage-point accuracy loss under ±300 ms jitter and irrelevant-gesture swaps.
How would we investigate whether the gesture swaps preserve referent-bearing motion while the adversarial training reduces speaker cues under timing jitter?

The plan is to train ShiftGuard and swap/adversary ablations on speaker-disjoint GestureRef. Then measure accuracy gains over speech-only models, speaker-probe accuracy, and accuracy losses under ±300-ms audiovisual offsets and irrelevant-gesture substitutions. This is a planned evaluation, not a report of results.
What does speaker-disjoint mean in this plan?

It means keeping speakers separate across the training and evaluation portions, so evaluation concerns speakers not seen in training. That matters because the question is whether ShiftGuard can use reference-bearing gesture information without relying on correlations tied to familiar speakers. The plan does not specify how many speakers or examples are involved.
Why train ablations as well as ShiftGuard?

The swap/adversary ablations are meant to help examine the roles of the gesture-swap and speaker-adversarial elements, rather than looking only at ShiftGuard as a whole. The plan calls for those ablations, but does not give their exact configurations or predict their results.
Would an ablation tell us by itself that a particular component caused an accuracy gain?

It could inform how performance differs when the swap or adversarial element is ablated, but the plan alone establishes no effect or causal conclusion. We would need the measurements before saying whether either element helped, hurt, or made no detectable difference.
What exactly is being measured against speech-only models?

The plan calls for measuring ShiftGuard’s accuracy gain relative to speech-only models on speaker-disjoint GestureRef. That comparison asks whether the speech–gesture approach improves reference resolution beyond speech alone for unseen speakers. No gain has yet been measured in this node.
Is speaker-probe accuracy another way of measuring reference-resolution accuracy?

No. Reference-resolution accuracy concerns which referent the system identifies. Speaker-probe accuracy concerns how well speaker identity can be recovered from the information being probed. Including both measurements lets the evaluation consider reference performance alongside the presence of speaker cues; the plan does not specify a probe design.
If the speaker-probe accuracy is low, would that settle the question?

Not by itself. A probe result would speak to recoverable speaker information under that probe, but it would not show whether ShiftGuard still uses referent-bearing motion. The planned speech-only comparison, ablations, and perturbation-loss measurements address other parts of the question.
Could strong reference accuracy alone show that identity cues were removed?

No. Strong reference accuracy would not, on its own, distinguish use of meaningful gesture motion from reliance on speaker-related correlations. That is why the plan includes speaker-disjoint evaluation, speaker-probe accuracy, and swap/adversary ablations rather than only an overall accuracy figure.
How will the timing concern be represented?

The plan measures accuracy loss under audiovisual offsets of ±300 milliseconds—timing displacement in either direction. That tests whether reference resolution remains stable when the speech and gesture are not perfectly aligned. The node does not specify a particular schedule of offsets or a calculation beyond measuring the resulting loss.
Does ±300 ms mean only two measurements, one at each endpoint?

Not necessarily. The plan names the ±300-ms offset condition but does not specify exactly which offsets within it are measured or how they are aggregated. It would be an added procedural detail to claim that only the two endpoints are used.
And what do the irrelevant-gesture measurements check?

They measure accuracy loss when an irrelevant gesture is substituted. The point is to see whether a visual change that should not determine the referent disrupts resolution. That differs from the label-updated relevant-gesture swaps used in the training proposal, where the gesture bears on the reference.
Are the timing offsets and irrelevant gestures necessarily tested together?

The plan calls for measuring ±300-ms and irrelevant-gesture losses, but it does not say whether those conditions are applied separately, simultaneously, or both. We should not add a combined test procedure that the plan has not specified.
Would the swap ablations only be judged by the irrelevant-gesture loss?

The plan does not restrict an ablation to a single measurement. It names swap/adversary ablations and a set of measurements—speech-only gains, speaker-probe accuracy, and the two perturbation losses—without assigning one metric exclusively to one ablation.
How do these measurements bear on the question of preserving referent-bearing motion?

The speech-only comparison examines whether gesture adds useful information for reference resolution on speaker-disjoint GestureRef. The swap ablations can help examine the role of the gesture-swap element, while the irrelevant-gesture loss checks whether non-referential gesture changes unduly affect accuracy. Together they bear on the question, but none is, by itself, a direct claim that the intended motion has been preserved.
And how does the adversary side enter the evaluation?

The plan includes adversary ablations and speaker-probe accuracy. Those offer ways to examine the speaker-adversarial element and the recoverability of speaker identity cues. Their results would need to be considered alongside reference-resolution performance: reducing speaker cues would not be sufficient if useful gesture information were also lost.
So there is no speaker-probe result yet?
Correct. Measuring speaker-probe accuracy is part of the plan. No probe accuracy, speech-only gain, ablation outcome, or perturbation loss is reported here.
Could we specify from this plan what speaker-probe accuracy would count as acceptable?

No acceptable speaker-probe threshold is stated. The plan says to measure that accuracy, not what numerical result would settle the identity-cue question. Assigning a threshold would add a criterion that is not in this node.
Does this plan require a particular architecture or training recipe for the ablations?

It does not specify one. It calls for training ShiftGuard and swap/adversary ablations on speaker-disjoint GestureRef, then taking the named measurements. Details of the architecture, exact ablation setups, and measurement procedures are not supplied.
Can you state the plan in one sentence without implying the experiment has already happened?

Train ShiftGuard and swap/adversary ablations on speaker-disjoint GestureRef, then measure gains over speech-only models, speaker-probe accuracy, and accuracy losses under ±300-ms audiovisual offsets and irrelevant-gesture substitutions.
What is the evaluation activity for ShiftGuard?

Evaluate ShiftGuard and its swap/adversary ablations on speaker-disjoint GestureRef. The activity covers three measurements: referent accuracy compared with speech-only, speaker-probe accuracy, and accuracy degradation under irrelevant-gesture swaps and ±300-ms audiovisual offsets. This describes what to evaluate; it does not report any outcomes.
What does referent accuracy mean in that list?

It concerns whether the system identifies the intended referent. Comparing that accuracy with speech-only performance asks whether ShiftGuard adds value beyond speech for reference resolution. The activity does not give an accuracy value for either system.
Why does the evaluation need speaker-disjoint GestureRef?

Speaker-disjoint evaluation keeps speakers in the evaluation portion distinct from those used for training. That makes performance on speakers not seen during training relevant to the question of whether reference resolution depends on speaker-specific correlations. The activity does not specify the number of speakers or how the split is constructed.
If ShiftGuard performs well against speech-only, does that alone show it is not using speaker cues?

No. A referent-accuracy comparison addresses reference-resolution performance, not by itself which cues the system uses. Speaker-disjoint evaluation and speaker-probe accuracy examine different aspects of the speaker-cue concern, while the ablations allow comparisons involving the swap and adversarial elements.
What is speaker-probe accuracy measuring here?

It concerns how accurately speaker identity can be recovered by a probe from the information it is given. That is distinct from referent accuracy: a model might identify referents accurately while still retaining information associated with who is speaking. The activity names speaker-probe accuracy but does not specify the probe or what score to expect.
Should I interpret lower speaker-probe accuracy as proof that referent-bearing motion has been preserved?

No. Speaker-probe accuracy speaks to recoverable speaker information under the probe; it does not directly establish that useful gesture motion remains available for resolving references. Referent accuracy and the swap/adversary ablations provide other parts of the evaluation.
What are the swap/adversary ablations doing in this activity?

They are versions of the evaluation involving ablation of the swap and adversarial elements. Comparing them with ShiftGuard can help examine how those elements relate to the named measurements. The activity does not define the exact ablation configurations or state what any comparison will show.
Could we assign one metric to the swap ablation and another to the adversary ablation?

The activity does not make that assignment. It says to evaluate ShiftGuard and the swap/adversary ablations using referent accuracy versus speech-only, speaker-probe accuracy, and degradation under the stated perturbations. Restricting a particular ablation to a particular metric would add a procedure not specified here.
What does the irrelevant-swap degradation measurement ask?

It asks how much referent accuracy degrades when an irrelevant gesture is swapped. Because the gesture is irrelevant to the reference, the measurement concerns sensitivity to a visual change that should not determine the referent. The activity calls for measuring degradation but reports no amount.
Is an irrelevant swap the same thing as swapping a referent-bearing gesture and updating its label?

No. An irrelevant-gesture swap is a perturbation for measuring degradation when the gesture does not bear on the reference. A label-updated relevant-gesture swap involves gesture content that does bear on the reference. Treating the two as identical would lose the distinction the evaluation needs.
What does the ±300-ms measurement cover?

It covers degradation when audiovisual timing is offset by up to 300 milliseconds in either direction. The evaluation asks whether referent accuracy holds up when speech and gesture are not aligned at one exact time. It does not specify which offsets are used within that range or give a measured loss.
Does the activity require testing irrelevant swaps and timing offsets together?

It names degradation under irrelevant swaps and under ±300-ms offsets, but does not specify whether the perturbations are applied separately, together, or both. The evaluation can be described faithfully without assuming a combined condition.
What accuracy is the degradation compared against?

The activity says to measure degradation, but does not define its comparison condition in detail. We can say it assesses the loss in accuracy under the stated perturbations without inventing a particular reference score or calculation.
Can this evaluation address the hypothesis about ShiftGuard without assuming it is true?

Yes. Referent accuracy versus speech-only addresses the predicted benefit from gesture-related information; speaker-probe accuracy bears on speaker cues; and irrelevant-swap and ±300-ms degradation address robustness. These are measurements to take, not evidence in advance for any predicted outcome.
Would one favorable measurement be enough to describe the whole evaluation as successful?

One measurement would cover only its own aspect. For example, referent accuracy would not replace speaker-probe accuracy, and neither would replace the perturbation-degradation measurements. This activity calls for all of them across ShiftGuard and the swap/adversary ablations; it does not report a judgment about success.
Do we have any results from the speaker probe or the offsets at this point?

No results are supplied in this activity. It specifies evaluating speaker-probe accuracy and degradation under ±300-ms offsets, along with the other named measurements, without stating observed values or conclusions.
Please restate the activity plainly, keeping it distinct from a result.

Evaluate ShiftGuard and swap/adversary ablations on speaker-disjoint GestureRef by measuring referent accuracy against speech-only, speaker-probe accuracy, and accuracy degradation under irrelevant-gesture swaps and ±300-ms audiovisual offsets.
What results were reported for ShiftGuard on unseen-speaker GestureRef?

Referent accuracy was 76%, compared with 64% for speech-only. The reported accuracy losses were 3 percentage points under irrelevant-gesture swaps and 4 percentage points under ±300-ms audiovisual jitter. Binary speaker-probe accuracy was 52%.
How large is the referent-accuracy difference?
It is 12 percentage points: 76% minus 64%. That is an absolute difference between the two reported accuracy rates, not a 12% relative increase.
Does “unseen-speaker GestureRef” apply to the accuracy comparison?
Yes. The reported 76% referent accuracy and the 64% speech-only accuracy are presented as the comparison on unseen-speaker GestureRef. No separate accuracy figures for individual speakers are given.
What does referent accuracy tell us here?

It reports how often the intended referent was identified correctly. In these findings, the ShiftGuard figure is 76%, and the speech-only comparison is 64%. Those figures describe reference-resolution accuracy, not speaker identification.
Are the 3 and 4 points both timing losses?
No. The 3-percentage-point loss is reported for irrelevant-gesture swaps. The 4-percentage-point loss is reported for ±300-ms audiovisual jitter. They correspond to different perturbations.
